  default, it became familiar to generations of Unix and Unix-like users. Bash’s prominence
write a detailed 800-word essay about the history of unix shells, no tools
  also meant that scripts written for it became a major part of system administration and
  software development.

  Meanwhile, the C shell’s successor, tcsh, expanded its interactive features and improved
  compatibility. Other shells emerged with different priorities. The Almquist shell, or ash,
  was small and suitable for systems with limited resources. Dash, a descendant of ash,
  became a fast implementation of the POSIX shell language and is used in some Linux systems
  for startup scripts. Zsh, first released in 1990 by Paul Falstad, combined ideas from
  several earlier shells and gained a reputation for extensive customization, powerful
  completion, and sophisticated interactive features.

  Standards have helped maintain a common foundation amid this variety. POSIX specifies a
  portable shell language and behavior, drawing heavily on the Bourne shell and related
  developments. A script written to POSIX conventions can often run across different Unix-
  like systems, while a script that depends on Bash, zsh, or ksh extensions may need that
  particular interpreter. This distinction is why scripts often begin with a line identifying
  which shell should run them.

  Today, shells remain central even as graphical interfaces and cloud services have changed
  computing. They are used to administer servers, automate builds, inspect logs, manage
  containers, and connect tools in repeatable workflows. Newer shells, including fish,
  emphasize discoverability and user-friendly defaults, while PowerShell applies shell
  concepts to a different programming and system-management tradition.

  Across these generations, the shell has balanced two roles: a quick place to issue commands
  and a language for expressing repeatable work. Each influential shell added ideas that
  users came to expect, from scripting and pipelines to history and completion. The result is
  not one universal shell, but a family of interpreters shaped by different needs. Unix
  shells endure because they make programs composable and let people turn a sequence of
  commands into a tool of their own.
